summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex medical history including Crohn’s disease, multiple abdominal surgeries, and a port-a-cath was admitted for fever and worsening right upper quadrant abdominal pain following a routine port flush at home. She was diagnosed with a coagulase-negative staphylococcal catheter-associated bloodstream infection, treated with a two-week course of intravenous vancomycin, with subsequent negative blood cultures confirming resolution. During her hospitalization, she developed a right upper lobe infiltrate, managed as presumed pneumonia with antibiotics. Abdominal pain was evaluated with CT, colonoscopy, and barium enema, which showed no evidence of bowel obstruction or stricture, with findings attributed to chronic Crohn’s-related inflammation. She required a packed red blood cell transfusion for iron deficiency anemia and NG tube placement for symptomatic management of gastric distention, later advanced to a regular diet. Her pain and infection improved, and she was discharged home on oral antibiotics, with plans for outpatient follow-up and lab monitoring.
